issues.legal_issue: A female limited owner who was not in possession of inherited property when the Hindu Succession Act commenced did not become its absolute owner by operation of the Act.
material_facts: The widow inherited the property from her husband and made an earlier gift of it to her daughter.
The earlier decree prevented the widow from possessing the property after that gift.
The widow made a second gift after the Act commenced.
issues.conclusion: Because the widow was not in possession of the inherited property when the Act commenced, she did not become its absolute owner under section 14, and the later gift did not take effect as a disposition by an absolute owner.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14 applies to property possessed by a female Hindu; it does not make her an absolute owner of inherited property that she was not in possession of when the Act commenced. The Court treated this point as settled by its prior decisions.

predicates.inheritance_property_case: The dispute concerns property inherited by a female owner.
predicates.inherited_property_not_possessed_at_comm: The female owner was not in possession of the inherited property when the relevant law commenced.

issues.definition: If a dispute concerns inherited property that its female owner did not possess when the relevant law commenced, she does not acquire absolute title to that property.

issues.legal_issue: Succession to an estate held by a female limited owner opens when she dies, and the law then in force governs who succeeds to the estate, provided it had not already vested in another person.
material_facts: The last male owner died before the Hindu Succession Act commenced, and his widow inherited the estate as a limited owner.
The widow was not in possession of the property when the Act commenced because of the earlier gift and decree.
The widow made a second gift after the Act commenced and died afterward.
The appellants claimed as reversioners under the earlier customary law; the respondent was the daughter of the last male owner.
issues.conclusion: Succession opened when the widow died and was governed by section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, not by the earlier customary law. The appeal was dismissed because the appellants' reversionary interest was only a chance of succession, not a vested right.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Moniram Kolita v. Keri Kolitani and Duni Chand v. Anar Kali: succession to the last male owner's estate opens on the termination of the female limited owner's estate, and the heirs are determined as if the last male owner had died at that time. The words “dying intestate” in section 8 describe intestacy and do not make the section retrospective; section 6, by contrast, expressly refers to a male Hindu dying after commencement. The Court explained and distinguished Eramma v. Verrupanna, approved Banso v. Charan Singh and Kuldip Singh v. Karnail Singh, and overruled Kempiah v. Girigamma. It also relied on Eastend Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and Venkatachalam v. Bombay Dyeing & Manufacturing Co. Ltd. concerning the consequences of a legal fiction. A right that had already vested under the earlier law could not be divested.

predicates.limited_owner_succession_case: The proceeding concerns who succeeds to an estate after the death of a female limited owner.
predicates.limited_owner_inherited_last_owner_estat: A female limited owner held the estate by succeeding to its last full owner.
predicates.limited_owner_died_after_legal_change: The female limited owner died after a change in the law governing succession had taken effect.
predicates.claimants_had_no_vested_right: The competing claimants held only a contingent chance of succession before the female limited owner died.

issues.definition: When a female limited owner inherited an estate and dies after a change in succession law, the law in force at her death governs succession if the competing claimants had no vested right.
